Dear reviewer,

As the end of the discussion period is approaching, we kindly ask that the reviewer to look at our rebuttal and give us any further questions which they have so that we can respond in time.

We thank the reviewer for their positive assessment of our work and theoretical results. We  address each of the raised points below.

---

> **1. The analysis is not very rigorous, especially in terms of analyzing the node information quality. There are many aspects to it, the label noise rate, the representation capability of the model etc. These aspects are overlooked in the analysis.**

Our results indeed address the mentioned factors in a generic sense. Note that in our general formulation, all types of node-level signals are captured by the loss functions $f_v$ and the search space $\Theta$, in a unified way. Our assumptions (4.3 and 4.4.) on these terms reflect the effect of the mentioned factors. In particular, imperfections in node information (including label noise) are represented by the gradient-variability parameter $\rho$, while model expressiveness is controlled by the R-separability assumption. This general form can then be specialized to any particular choice of features, labels, or noise model, the case study in the paper being just one of them. Together, these two assumptions give a clear and measurable description of node-information quality.

---

> **2. It is unclear why the atomic norm concept has been used instead of nuclear norm. I did not understand any advantages to this aspect. What would be the challenges in using nuclear norm directly as in (1) which is more common in graph clustering algorithms?**

The atomic norm is a direct generalization of the nuclear norm, and this generalization is what makes it possible to incorporate node features into our model.  With the nuclear norm alone, the atoms are fixed to rank-one matrices of the form $\mathbf{e}\mathbf{e}^\top$, which only capture graph structure. In our setting, we need atoms that also include node-feature terms so that the optimization can couple structure and node information. The atomic-norm view lets us define these augmented atoms in a  principled way, while still keeping the same convex-optimization machinery used in graph clustering. Note that removing the feature specific terms makes our framework a standard nuclear norm formulation again, since the atomic norm of rank-1 matrices is indeed the nuclear norm. 

---

> **3. The overall optimization problem (6) is not nonconvex even though it is built on the convex graph clustering problem. So, there is no discussion on the issue of multiple optimal solutions if there is any.**

Although our recovery guarantees do not rely on uniqueness of the optimizer, only on the existence of an optimal solution with the desired block structure, we note that SON-regularized problems can admit unique solutions under additional conditions; see the analysis of Rahbar et al. [1]. Exploring such uniqueness conditions for our specific formulation is certainly possible, but it is orthogonal to the main contributions of the paper which is to theoretically quantify the synergy between node classification and spectral clustering.

[1] Rahbar et al., "Recovery Bounds on Class-Based Optimal Transport: A Sum-of-Norms Regularization Framework,'' ICML 2023.

---

> **4. In Theorem 4.5, there is no influence of $\mu_0$? Is it expected?**

Yes, this is expected. As shown in the appendix (page 15), when we write the optimization problem explicitly, the constraint $L_{vv}=1$ for all $v$ (which is part of the definition of $\mathcal{B}$ in (1)) forces the atomic coefficients to sum to $n$. This makes the $\mu_0 \sum_i \lambda_i$ term a constant across all feasible solutions, so it does not influence the conditions in Theorem 4.5. To avoid confusion in the main text, we kept the general form of $\mathcal{B}$.

----

> **5. Also it is unclear how does $K$  not influence the recovery in Part 2 of Theorem 4.5? What is the rationale?**

In Part 2 of Theorem 4.5, perfect recovery depends only on the condition
$
\rho \le \gamma n_i,
$
where $n_i$ is the size of each cluster. Since $n_i$ can be written roughly as $n/K$ for a fixed total number of nodes n, the number of clusters $K$ affects the bound only through $n_i.$ As $K$ increases, each cluster becomes smaller, and therefore the allowable within-cluster variability $\rho$ also becomes smaller. This is why the condition does not explicitly depend on $K$: the effect of $K$ is already absorbed through the cluster size $n_i$.

Dear reviewer,

As the end of the discussion period is approaching, we kindly ask that the reviewer to look at our rebuttal and give us any further questions which they have so that we can respond in time.

For clarity, we restate our main contributions:

- A new convex atomic-norm formulation that jointly incorporates graph structure, node features, and partial labels.

- Deterministic perfect-recovery guarantees that explicitly establish the bidirectional benefit (graph improves classification and features improve clustering) and show that their integration leads to strictly weaker recovery conditions than using either source alone. These guarantees hold at the level of the optimization problem itself and do not depend on any particular algorithm or initialization. These results are fundamentally different from prior CSBM-based analyses, as detailed in our previous response.

- A conditional-gradient solver enabling computation of solutions in a polynomial time, used for validating the theoretical recovery trends.


---

We hope these clarifications address the concerns regarding novelty and contribution.
We would be happy to provide further details if needed, and we kindly ask the reviewer to ***reconsider their evaluation*** in light of this explanation.

> **6. The experiments are limited to only synthetic scenario. The feasibility of the proposed algorithm for large scale clustering and also comparison with existing methods is lacking.**

The goal of the paper is primarily theoretical, and the experiments are designed to validate our theory. Full large-scale empirical study and comparison with existing methods is beyond the scope of this submission. 

---

> **7. There is no discussion about the missingness of node information and also the missingness of edge information per node. How do the results and the algorithm get adapted to these real scenarios?**

Our analysis assumes fully observed features and graph structure in order to avoid complexity in the theoretical setting. Extending the framework to missing-node or missing-edge scenarios would require additional modeling assumptions and a different recovery analysis, which is outside the scope of this paper. We will mention this as a natural future direction.

---

> **8. How does the algorithm/theory support multiple node membership as in the MMSB model? The missingness parameter may have some connection to this model, I assume. The results do not look obvious and it would be good to see some discussions around these challenging scenarios.**

Our optimization framework can already handle soft or probabilistic memberships, since the label information enters only through the node-level losses $f_v$, which can be defined for mixed-membership labels. In fact, our case study uses a probabilistic labeling model, and we have already showed that our model is suitable for mixed-membership labels.

We thank the reviewer for their positive assessment of our work. Regarding the two weaknesses, we were not able to verify the connection between them and the problem setup or contributions of our paper. We briefly clarify this below.

---

> **Several results rely on strong simplifying assumptions, such as feature distributions being Gaussian, perfect label smoothness, or orthogonality between eigenvectors. These conditions may not hold in realistic graphs, making the theoretical guarantees partially idealized. The authors may need to elaborate on this.**

Our theoretical results do not rely on the specific simplifying assumptions mentioned by the reviewer. The core analysis is carried out in a fully deterministic framework with arbitrary convex node-level losses $f_v$ and a general feasible set $\Theta$, which are only required to satisfy Assumptions 4.3 and 4.4. This generic setup can be instantiated with any feature model, label model, or noise model; the case study in the paper is only one example. The recovery guarantees therefore do not depend on Gaussianity, perfect smoothness, or orthogonality assumptions.

---

> **The authors suggest their framework could generalize to “all permutation-invariant graph models” and “guide the design of universal GNN architectures”. Could the authors provide more evidence on this point?**

We note that the statements mentioned by the reviewer do not appear in our paper. We do not make claims about “all permutation-invariant graph models” or about “guiding the design of universal GNN architectures.” These points are therefore not related to the contributions or scope of our work.

summary.value: This paper develops theoretical limits on node classification accuracy for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by characterizing when perfect node classification is achievable under different graph and feature conditions. The authors formalize a new framework based on information bottleneck principles and spectral graph theory to derive upper and lower bounds on classification performance. The analysis covers both homophilic and heterophilic graphs, revealing that feature–label alignment and graph smoothness jointly determine the attainable accuracy. They further propose tight bounds for message-passing GNNs and show that deeper layers can asymptotically saturate or even degrade the achievable accuracy, depending on the graph topology. Synthetic experiments and controlled real-world datasets (Cora, Citeseer, Chameleon, Squirrel) confirm that the empirical performance of standard GNNs (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE) aligns with the derived theoretical limits.

strengths.value:
Three strong points are:

1. The paper establishes novel upper and lower bounds on perfect node classification for GNNs, offering fundamental insights into when 100% accuracy is theoretically attainable. The use of spectral decomposition and information-theoretic analysis provides mathematical depth and rigor.

2. Unlike many theoretical works that focus solely on homophilic graphs, this paper’s framework systematically handles both homophilic and heterophilic regimes, explaining observed empirical gaps in GNN performance across benchmark datasets.

3. The authors conduct careful synthetic and real-data experiments showing that practical model performance adheres closely to the predicted bounds, validating the theoretical predictions and demonstrating good interpretability.

weaknesses.value:
Two weak points:

1. Several results rely on strong simplifying assumptions, such as feature distributions being Gaussian, perfect label smoothness, or orthogonality between eigenvectors. These conditions may not hold in realistic graphs, making the theoretical guarantees partially idealized. The authors may need to elaborate on this.

2. The authors suggest their framework could generalize to “all permutation-invariant graph models” and “guide the design of universal GNN architectures”. Could the authors provide more evidence on this point?

summary.value: This paper introduces a novel convex optimization framework for transductive node classification that unifies graph clustering and node-specific information via atomic norm regularization. The authors provide rigorous theoretical guarantees for perfect label recovery under different regimes, demonstrating that combining modalities leads to strictly milder recovery conditions. They also propose an efficient alternating conditional gradient algorithm and validate their theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic data.

strengths.value: The core strength is the novel convex optimization framework that formally unifies graph clustering and node classification using atomic norms and sum-of-norms regularization. The theoretical analysis is rigorous and provides the first, to my knowledge, formal conditions demonstrating the synergistic benefit of combining graph structure and node information for perfect classification recovery.

weaknesses.value:
- Practical relevance: The entire theoretical and empirical validation is based on a highly specific synthetic case study. The paper fails to demonstrate the framework's effectiveness or scalability on standard, large-scale, real-world graph datasets (e.g., typical OGB or Planetoid datasets used for GNNs), making it difficult to assess its practical utility compared to established heuristic GNN approaches.
- Computational complexity vs. GNNs: The paper highlights the theoretical tractability but then immediately pivots to the non-convex, fixed-rank CADO approximation due to computational expense. The complexity analysis of CADO is weak; stating it is "efficient and practical" without concrete runtime comparisons or complexity analysis relative to modern GNNs is insufficient. The practical advantage of CADO over spectral clustering or GNNs is not clearly established.
- Loss generalization: While the framework is designed for general convex loss functions, the recovery guarantees and the practical CADO implementation rely on a specific Gaussian/label-entropy loss structure. It is unclear how the derived recovery conditions would generalize or if CADO would remain efficient for arbitrary convex losses.

questions.value:
- How does the runtime and memory footprint of the CADO algorithm compare against spectral clustering and a standard GNN (like GCN or GraphSAGE) when applied to large, real-world graphs (e.g., millions of edges)?
- Could the authors provide experimental results using standard node classification benchmarks (e.g., Cora, PubMed, or any OGB dataset) to demonstrate the competitive performance and scalability of the proposed framework beyond the synthetic SBM/Gaussian case study?
- What guarantees or empirical evidence can be provided regarding the quality of the fixed-rank solution relative to the global optimum of the full convex problem?

summary.value: This paper proposes a new method to solve the node classification task on graphs with node features and labels. The authors formulate the problem as a constrained convex optimization problem which jointly optimizes the alignment in graph structure as well as node features and partial labels. The authors show that, under certain assumptions on the graph structure and the node feature vectors, their method can perfectly recover the ground-truth node labels. The authors also provide a conditional gradient method to solve a particular case of the optimization problem under low rank assumption.

strengths.value: The convex optimization formulation is new. Other than that, I am not sure what to say. I welcome the authors to further elaborate the strengths and contributions of the paper.

weaknesses.value: I find it hard to identify a solid contribution of this work. If I treat it as a methodology paper for solving the node classification task on graphs with node features and partial labels, it is missing an important comparison with state-of-the-art methods that are based on graph neural networks. And in practice, I doubt that the proposed methods would be better than GNNs. If I treat it as a theory paper, the theoretical setup, and in particular the assumptions, are difficult to parse. The authors claim that they provide the first rigorous theoretical result demonstrating that node features and graph structure can provably interact to improve node classification. This is clearly not the case, given prior work on node classification in the Contextual Stochastic Block Model (e.g., Braun et al. An iterative clustering algorithm for the Contextual Stochastic Block Model with optimality guarantees). The authors should discuss the assumptions of the theoretical setup and how they are related to other theoretical setups such as those considered in the analysis of CSBM. Basically, the assumptions in this work requires both the graph structure and the node feature vectors have enough signal. This is intuitively similar to those required in CSBM. Because of this I find it hard to identify new theoretical insights offered in this work.

We thank the reviewer for their feedback. We address each of the raised points below.

---

> **Practical relevance: The entire theoretical and empirical validation is based on a highly specific synthetic case study. The paper fails to demonstrate the framework's effectiveness or scalability on standard, large-scale, real-world graph datasets (e.g., typical OGB or Planetoid datasets used for GNNs), making it difficult to assess its practical utility compared to established heuristic GNN approaches.**

The goal of the paper is to establish rigorous perfect-recovery guarantees for transductive node classification by combining graph structure, node features, and partial labels within a single convex formulation. The algorithmic part is included only to provide an empirical check of the theoretical recovery conditions, not to propose a new scalable method for real-world deployment.

Our intention was not to design an algorithm that competes with GNN-based node-classification methods or to benchmark performance on large OGB or Planetoid datasets. Instead, the purpose of our algorithm is to confirm that the synergy between graph clustering and node classification—proved in our theory—also appears in a practical solver. In other words, the algorithm is a proof-of-concept that avoids brute-force enumeration and shows that the ideal solution described in Section 4.1 is indeed attainable by a reasonable procedure.

---

> **Computational complexity vs. GNNs: The paper highlights the theoretical tractability but then immediately pivots to the non-convex, fixed-rank CADO approximation due to computational expense. The complexity analysis of CADO is weak; stating it is "efficient and practical" without concrete runtime comparisons or complexity analysis relative to modern GNNs is insufficient. The practical advantage of CADO over spectral clustering or GNNs is not clearly established.**

As mentioned earlier, comparing the computational complexity of our method with GNNs or spectral clustering is outside the scope of this work. The purpose of our algorithm is not to provide a faster or more scalable alternative to these methods. Instead, CADO is designed to efficiently identify the optimal atoms that minimize objective (6) without resorting to brute-force search, which would be computationally infeasible.

Importantly, in GNNs the low-rank embeddings $\mathbf{e}_i$ and the model parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_i$ are merged into a single parametric function and cannot be separated. Because of this coupling, it is not possible to determine the exact conditions under which a GNN achieves perfect recovery in the sense defined in Section 4.1. For this reason, we could not use GNNs to validate our theoretical results, and the role of CADO is solely to confirm that the perfect-recovery conditions hold for a practical solver that directly optimizes our objective.


---

> **Loss generalization: While the framework is designed for general convex loss functions, the recovery guarantees and the practical CADO implementation rely on a specific Gaussian/label-entropy loss structure. It is unclear how the derived recovery conditions would generalize or if CADO would remain efficient for arbitrary convex losses.**

We agree that other loss functions could also be used in the experimental setting, and we will include additional results with alternative losses in the revised version. However, as shown in Section 5, the CADO algorithm is derived for any convex loss function. The algorithm itself does not rely on the Gaussian or label-entropy structure—it only requires convexity to compute the LMOs and perform the updates. The Gaussian-based case study in the experiments is simply one example that allows us to illustrate the behavior of the method in a controlled setting.

More importantly, Theorem 4.5 already provides recovery guarantees for general convex loss functions. The case study is included only to demonstrate the synergistic effect of objective (6) in practice, not to restrict the framework to a specific loss choice.

We thank the reviewer for their feedback. We would like to clarify two points:
- As indicated in the title and throughout the analysis, this work is a theoretical paper.  
- The theoretical contributions we establish are not covered by prior CSBM-based works, whose theoretical contributions is critically limited for node classification as we discuss in the following.

---


**Theoretical scope of the paper:**

The objective of the paper is to establish rigorous perfect-recovery guarantees for transductive node classification by integrating graph structure, node features, and partial labels within a single convex framework. The algorithmic component is included to strengthen our theoretical result by demonstrating that the recovery is attainable with a polynomial algorithm (due to convexity of our framework). Indeed, this algorithm is not intended to be scalable in real-world applications and proposing a scalable version of this algorithm for real-world applications (and not only polynomial) falls beyond our scope. The empirical results in the paper merely serve as an evidence to support the trends predicted by the theoretical analysis.

As a theoretical work, we are focused on establishing provable limits and deterministic worst-case guarantees. Our objective is fundamentally different from heuristic GNN approaches, focused on scalability to maximize the empirical performance. Therefore, a comparison with GNNs is unfair and outside the scope of this paper.

---

**Relation to CSBM-based methods such as Braun et al. [1]:**

As already mentioned in our paper (related works), we acknowledge the relation of the CSBM literature to ours, as it also analyzes the benefits of combining features and structure. However, our work addresses a distinct problem setting and provides fundamentally different types of guarantees. In the following, we make these differences clear:

- **Novelty in Two-Way Interaction (Synergistic Effect) and Perfect Recovery.** 
A central contribution of our work is proving a two-way synergistic effect: node information improves graph-based recovery, and graph structure in turn improves *classification* beyond what features and labels alone achieve. Our recovery conditions become strictly milder when both sources of information are used jointly. CSBM-based analyses only establish one direction of this interaction—covariates improving *clustering*—and do not address the classification side of the problem. Thus, the synergistic perfect-recovery result we establish is not covered by CSBM theory.



- **Broader problem class.** To address node classification, we explicitly consider the task of training a classifier, called $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ by the loss terms $f_v$, which are convex, but otherwise arbitrary, and can model a wide range of classification tasks. As a result, our theory prdicts not only perfect clustering of the nodes but also the resulting classifier in Eq. (8). In contrast, CSBM-based works  only consider a Gaussian-mixture generative model. Importantly, Gaussian mixtures alone do not define a classification task, therefore CSBM-based methods do not solve node classification with partial labels. Hence, these results cannot be associated with the node classification problem. Further note that, the Gaussian mixture models, as in the CSBM-based methods, are a special case of the broader problem class we study.


- **General and Non-Asymptotic Results.** 
Our analysis applies to general convex losses and provides exact, non-asymptotic recovery guarantees in a fully deterministic setting, without any requirements on initialization. In contrast, CSBM-based results are probabilistic and asymptotic in nature and typically rely on careful initialization (see, e.g., Theorem 2 in Braun et al.). Moreover, those works primarily aim to design a specific clustering algorithm, and their theoretical results emerge as a by-product of that algorithm (check their second contribution). Their guarantees apply only to a specific generative model and a specific algorithm, whereas our results hold at the level of the optimization formulation and do not depend on any particular algorithm.


---

[1] Braun et al., "An iterative clustering algorithm for the Contextual Stochastic Block Model
with optimality guarantees," ICML 2022.

title.value: Final Clarifications for the Area Chair

comment.value:
Dear Area Chair,

As we did not receive any response from the reviewers, we would like to bring the following key points to your consideration. We believe there is no solid justification from Reviewer pc75 and Reviewer sh5y for rejecting the paper, and we addressed their concerns in detail within our individual responses. In our view, both reviewers ignored the main motivation and contribution of the paper and provided no detailed explanation for their assessment. In particular:

* **Reviewer pc75 missed the main differences between our setup and related CSBM literature that we had already cited.** The reviewer provided no further explanation regarding this point. CSBM does not address the classification task in node classification and hence does not focus on the synergy between clustering and classification. Its theory also depends on strong assumptions on initialization, which are unnecessary in our framework. Moreover, our analysis is in a deterministic setting, not probabilistic, which fits node classification better.

* **Reviewer sh5y completely ignores the theoretic aspect of our work and focuses on algorithmic aspects, which have not been the goal of this work.** Note that the algorithm in our paper serves to show that the suggested bounds can be achieved by polynomial-time algorithms (an aspect of the theoretical discussion), and it was not intended to suggest a practical node-classification method on a par with GNNs.

As these clarifications could not be discussed with the reviewers, we respectfully ask that you consider the rebuttal carefully when evaluating the paper. We believe our responses resolve the central issues raised in the reviews.


Thank you for your time and consideration.

Best Regards, Authors

> **How does the runtime and memory footprint of the CADO algorithm compare against spectral clustering and a standard GNN (like GCN or GraphSAGE) when applied to large, real-world graphs (e.g., millions of edges)?**


As stated in the previous response, we did not design CADO to compete with GNNs or spectral clustering. Howvere, the runtime and efficiency of the algorithm can be characterized in terms of the LMO solvers (14) and (15) in the paper. The LMO in (15) is quite cheap, since it decomposes into n independent optimization problems (one per node), with total complexity on the order of $\mathcal{O}(nK)$, where K is the number of clusters. For the LMO in (14), the complexity depends on the choice of loss function and cannot be fixed in full generality. In the Gaussian case study, the LMO requires an eigendecomposition of the covariance-gradient matrix R, which costs $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$, where d is the feature dimension and typically $d \ll n$. Overall, the per-run complexity of CADO in this setting is on the order of
$\mathcal{O}\big(T (nK + d^3)\big)$, where T is the number of iterations.

For comparison, a standard spectral clustering pipeline on a sparse graph with n nodes, m edges, and K clusters typically has time complexity
$\mathcal{O}\big(mK + nK^2\big)$
for computing the top K eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, with memory on the order of $\mathcal{O}(m + nK)$.

Similarly, a typical GNN such as GCN or GraphSAGE with hidden dimension $d_h$, $L$ layers, and trained for $E$ epochs has total training complexity roughly
$\mathcal{O}\big(E L (m d_h + n d_h^2)\big)$,
with memory on the order of $\mathcal{O}(m + n d_h)$.

These expressions clarify that CADO’s cost is dominated by the linear term in $nK$ plus a feature-dimension term $d^3$, while spectral clustering and GNNs scale primarily with the number of edges m and the embedding dimension. Our focus in this work, however, is not to optimize these trade-offs against GNNs, but to provide a practical solver that can realize the perfect-recovery guarantees of our convex framework.

---

> **Could the authors provide experimental results using standard node classification benchmarks (e.g., Cora, PubMed, or any OGB dataset) to demonstrate the competitive performance and scalability of the proposed framework beyond the synthetic SBM/Gaussian case study?**

The main purpose of the experimental section is to demonstrate the synergistic behavior of the objective function across a wide range of noise levels and misconnection rates. For this reason, the experiments focus on controlled synthetic settings where the theoretical conditions can be directly verified. Comparing the performance or scalability of CADO against GNNs on benchmark datasets is outside the scope of the paper, since the goal is not to develop a competitive node-classification algorithm, but to validate the perfect-recovery guarantees of our framework.

---

> **What guarantees or empirical evidence can be provided regarding the quality of the fixed-rank solution relative to the global optimum of the full convex problem?**

We do not claim a formal equivalence between the full convex problem and its fixed-atom nonconvex variant. However, there is a natural rationale for why the solutions are expected to coincide. The sum-of-norms term in (6) implicitly limits the number of active atoms in any optimal solution of the convex problem. Our nonconvex formulation exploits exactly this structure by directly searching over a finite set of atoms. In practice, we observe that the algorithm consistently identifies the same atoms predicted by the theory, and the resulting solution matches the convex optimum in all our experiments.

---

We hope these clarifications address the reviewer's concerns. We would be happy to provide further details if needed, and we kindly ask the reviewer to ***reconsider their evaluation*** in light of this explanation.
